analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate prices for brand-name drugs that face no competition.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote, never gained a single cosponsor, and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, the government is barred from interfering when drug companies negotiate prices with the private insurance plans that run Medicare's prescription drug benefit. This bill would carve out an exception for single-source drugs and biologics — drugs with no generic competition — requiring Medicare to negotiate a maximum price directly with the manufacturer. If no deal is reached within 90 days, the government sets the price itself, based on the manufacturer's reported costs and what the drug costs under other government programs like the VA and Medicaid, and annual increases are capped at inflation.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who take brand-name drugs without generic or biosimilar competition — often the most expensive drugs in the program — would pay less at the pharmacy, and taxpayers would share in the savings since Medicare helps fund the drug benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare enrollees taking high-cost brand-name drugs

how_it_helps.text: Medicare would have to negotiate a maximum price for every covered single-source drug or biological, ending the current ban on government involvement in pricing for these drugs [S2] [S3].

If negotiation fails within 90 days, the government sets the price itself, using the manufacturer's reported costs and the prices already paid by the Department of Veterans Affairs and Medicaid as reference points [S3].
After the first year, the maximum price could only rise with inflation (the consumer price index), preventing annual price increases beyond that [S3].
A manufacturer's participation in negotiation would be a condition of Medicare covering its drugs at all, giving the government real leverage [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would see the prices they can charge Medicare plans capped, cutting into revenue on the drugs where they now face no competition.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers warned-style objection, supported by general economic reasoning: when a government buyer can set a price floor below what a company wants to charge, companies may earn less on new medicines, which can reduce the return on investment that funds research into new drugs. The bill acknowledges the tension by requiring the price-setter to weigh 'affordability and accessibility' of the drug, but a company facing a price it did not agree to would have less recourse [S3].

The bill leaves the private insurance structure of Medicare's drug benefit fully intact — plans keep their own formularies and can still negotiate discounts below the government-set price — so some of the negotiated savings would flow through private intermediaries rather than directly to beneficiaries [S3].

The price-setting backstop would take effect over a phased regulatory process: the Secretary had a year just to write rules identifying which drugs count as 'single source,' so savings would not appear immediately even if the bill became law [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare enrollees and taxpayers, the bill offers a direct mechanism to lower prices on the category of drugs least subject to market pressure, and it keeps the existing private-plan structure rather than replacing it. The real cost is borne by brand-name manufacturers, and the strongest objection — that government-set prices could dampen investment in new medicines — is a genuine trade-off rather than a flaw in design. The 90-day negotiation window with a government-set fallback and an inflation cap is a firm approach, and the bill's requirement that affordability and accessibility be weighed softens the risk that patients lose access.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late July 2018, referred to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees, and died there when the Congress ended in January 2019 — no hearing, no vote, no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on July 26, 2018, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees [S1] [S5].
Within days it was sent to the health subcommittees of both committees, where no further action was recorded [S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without the bill receiving any vote in committee or on the House floor [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept the status quo: Medicare is still barred from interfering in drug pricing, and no negotiation requirement ever took effect. The 2019-2020 Congress introduced a successor version that again went nowhere.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring Medicare to negotiate prices for single-source drugs and biologics, and proposed it late in the session when Congress had little working time left.

against.name: Rep. Greg Walden
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee holding one referral of the bill never took it up; it was referred to the Health Subcommittee and no markup or hearing followed.

against.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee holding the second referral of the bill never took it up; no action followed the subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call record exists; the bill's support was limited to one Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, and no Republican publicly championed it in the record.

industries.note: The bill would cap the price they can charge Medicare plans for their most protected products — drugs with no generic or biosimilar competition — and make participation in negotiation a condition of Medicare coverage. The industry's interest in preserving the current ban on government involvement runs directly against the interest of Medicare enrollees who pay those prices.

industries.industry: Medicare prescription drug plans (PDP sponsors and Medicare Advantage plans)
industries.note: The bill preserves their role entirely — they keep their formularies and can still negotiate discounts below the government-set maximum — while they would likely benefit from lower acquisition costs for the affected drugs.

Drugs that gain generic competition would be excluded from the government price-setting process, preserving the incentive for other manufacturers to bring competing versions to market, and cheaper alternatives to capped brand-name drugs would become more attractive.
